extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals and communications officers pitching b-roll to broadcast journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for PRs/communicators on producing and sharing b-roll (video footage) with busy broadcast journalists to increase the chances of coverage. Covers technical, editorial and pitching best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include b-roll with a pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: The story has a much better chance of being broadcast if it comes to the journalist with b-roll included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing b-roll is an opportunity to get your story seen by a larger audience; TV news is a visual medium and newsrooms with tight budgets and time constraints welcome supplied footage. Also consider offering b-roll to radio stations for their social media channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide footage journalists can't easily get
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can provide interesting b-roll that news desks will struggle to get for themselves, that can persuade desks to take up your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good examples: charity projects overseas, support workers at night on city streets, or other rare access. Anti-pattern: sending footage that is readily available or generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sending dull footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't send dull footage, but don't be afraid of the ordinary if it's the sort of thing news crews rarely film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise footage with narrative interest or unusual access rather than safe, uninspiring shots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply strong case studies, human drama and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: What sells is strong case studies, human drama, and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include subjects and scenes that convey emotion and human impact; examples include a video diary of a family depending on food banks. These elements make footage more usable and compelling for broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor the pitch to the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of who you're pitching to, what they need and the sort of stories they cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research the outlet and the journalist/editor’s remit. Target planning editors with short, relevant films rather than long detailed text. Make the pitch simple and brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of regulatory/reuse restrictions (Ofcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the Ofcom code means there are plenty of rules and restrictions on how submitted footage can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consent, rights clearance and any editorial restrictions are managed before sending footage. Don't assume all footage can be repurposed without permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filmed interviews/case studies help but expect editors to reshoot interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Filmed interviews and case studies can help news desks judge the merits of a story and see how interviewees present themselves, but most editors will want to shoot their own interviews and ask their own questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide interview material to illustrate the story and the subject's on-camera presence, but treat it as supplementary — news teams often prefer conducting their own interviews for editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a short video over a long press release
rubrics_metrics.description: You've got much more chance of a planning editor watching a two-minute film than reading a two-page press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep audiovisual pitches concise; lead with short, tightly edited films to capture attention in a busy newsroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold each shot for 7–10 seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: When filming, hold each shot for 7-10 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives editors enough usable frames to cut between shots. If you cannot stop the camera shaking, add some gentle, deliberate movement rather than letting it be shaky — deliberate movement is preferable to shaky shots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer wide shots for editing flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can control how wide an angle you have on your camera, try and shoot most of your shots wide (i.e. avoid too many unnecessary close ups, unless essential to your story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide shots make editing easier and provide context. Use close-ups only when they add specific value to the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoot a variety of shots to illustrate the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoot a variety of shots to illustrate your story. They may not all be used by the journalist but at least give them the option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover all aspects of the story and provide options for editors by varying scale, perspective and action; redundancy is better than missing a needed angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let action unfold naturally; avoid excessive zooming
rubrics_metrics.description: Try and let the action unfold in front of you. Don’t zoom in and out trying to cover every piece of the story in one go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture sustained takes of the action rather than frantic zooming; longer, steady observations are more useful in editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film smartphones in landscape orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: If filming with your smartphone, film in landscape (not portrait) i.e. film with the phone on its side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape matches broadcast and web video formats; portrait footage is difficult to use in most broadcast contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit supplied b-roll to ~5 minutes and compile as one file
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, don’t send the journalist more than five minutes of b-roll as they will appreciate you having only sent them relevant shots. Send the b-roll as one file, with shots compiled together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the package focused so journalists don't have to wade through hours of footage. Compile shots into a single file but keep each shot separate within the file; do not use artistic fades between shots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clean footage without subtitles or added graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strip off any subtitles or added graphics from your footage. A broadcaster will only really be able to use ‘clean’ footage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver raw/clean files to allow broadcasters to add their own graphics and captions. Embedded text or graphics can limit editorial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send highest resolution available via cloud storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Send the highest resolution footage you have, whether that’s HD or 4K using a cloud storage system such as Google Drive, WeTransfer or Dropbox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher resolution gives journalists more options in framing and cropping; with a five-minute limit file sizes should be manageable. Use reputable cloud transfer services and provide clear download links.
